opus-5.5.text:
Thanks for having me. Honestly, what changed most for me was realizing how much a clean-looking scaling curve hides about what's actually going on inside the model.

Going in, I had the standard picture in my head: you add compute, data, or parameters, and loss goes down smoothly along a power law. That's true at the level of aggregate loss, and it's a remarkably robust empirical regularity. But when we started looking at specific behaviors, things like in-context learning or how models pick up a particular capability, the story got much messier and more interesting. Underneath that smooth aggregate curve you see lots of individual mechanisms forming, competing, sometimes appearing fairly abruptly, and sometimes getting replaced by different strategies as the model gets bigger or trains longer.

So the first shift was moving from thinking of scaling laws as laws about *intelligence* to thinking of them as laws about *averages*. The loss is averaged over an enormous number of tokens and skills, and averaging tends to smooth things out. That doesn't make scaling laws wrong. It means they're the wrong tool if your question is "when will the model be able to do X?" or "how does it do X?"

The second shift, which comes from my interpretability background, was that I started wanting scaling laws for *mechanisms*, not just for loss. If you can model a behavior as the model implicitly inferring something, say which task it's being asked to do from the examples in the prompt, then you can sometimes write down a much more principled curve for how that behavior should change with more examples or more scale. That felt much more satisfying than fitting a power law and extrapolating, because the parameters of the curve actually mean something. You can ask why the curve has that shape, not just whether it fits.

And the third thing, which is a bit more humbling, is how sensitive these trends can be to setup. Choices about data, evaluation metric, and how you measure a capability can change whether something looks smooth or "emergent." That made me more skeptical of strong extrapolations in both directions, both "scaling will solve everything" and "scaling has hit a wall."

So if I had to sum it up: I still think scaling laws are one of the most important empirical findings in the field. But my own work convinced me they're a starting point for understanding, not an explanation. The real question is what's being learned along the curve, and that's where I think interpretability and scaling research really need each other.

r001.rationale: He attributes his changed understanding of scaling laws to examining behaviors in his own work, and says that work convinced him scaling laws are a starting point for understanding rather than an explanation.

fable-5.1.text:
Thanks for having me. I think the honest answer is that it made me a lot more humble about what scaling laws actually tell you.

Going in, I had the textbook picture in my head: you plot loss against compute on a log-log scale, you get a straight line, and the line tells you where things are headed. That picture is true, but it's true in a narrow sense. What the experiment taught me is that the smooth curve you see in loss is hiding a lot of structure underneath.

The specific thing that shifted my thinking was looking at individual capabilities rather than aggregate loss. When we actually tracked how models at different scales handled particular linguistic phenomena, the picture wasn't smooth at all. Some things improved gradually. Some things didn't move for a long time and then jumped. And a few things that we expected to improve with scale basically stayed flat, because the pretraining objective just doesn't push on them very hard. Loss averages all of that out, which is exactly why it looks so clean.

So the lesson wasn't that scaling laws are wrong. It's that loss is a very lossy summary of what a model can do. If you care about a specific behavior, the headline curve can't tell you whether more scale will fix it, or whether you need to change the data, the objective, or how you're probing the model in the first place.

The other thing it changed is how I think about where the interesting research is. A lot of the scaling story is about engineering: more data, more compute, same recipe. But the places where the curve bends, or doesn't bend when you'd expect it to, are where you actually learn something about how these models represent language. That's the part I find myself drawn to now, trying to understand mechanistically why a given capability shows up at a given scale, rather than just predicting that it will.

r001.rationale: The candidate says the experiment shifted his thinking and taught him that scaling laws’ smooth aggregate-loss curves conceal capability-level structure, clearly presenting his own experiment as the source of a substantive understanding.
